parts.title: Booking driving lessons
parts.context: A student phones a driving school to ask about lessons and prices.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a student phoning a driving school to ask about lessons. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: Good morning, Greenway Driving School, Paula speaking.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Hello. I'd like to start driving lessons, please. I want to learn in a manual car, not an automatic.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: No problem. Most of our learners do. Let me take a few details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants to learn in a manual car, so 'manual' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: joel
script.text: It's Joel Greenaway. That's G-R-E-E-N-A-W-A-Y. It's funny, because it's nearly the name of your school.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: So it is. And how old are you, Joel?

script.speaker: joel
script.text: I'm seventeen. I'll be eighteen in June, but I can already have a provisional licence.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: That's right. Have you had any lessons before?

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Yes, ten hours with another school, but then they closed down, so I need to carry on with someone new.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: I'm sorry to hear that. When would you like your lessons?

script.speaker: joel
script.text: After school, so Wednesdays, if possible. I have football practice on Tuesdays and Thursdays.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: Wednesday is fine. And which test centre would you like to use?

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Ashford, because that's the nearest to my home.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: Now, let me explain our packages. The Starter package is five hours, and it's thirty-five pounds an hour. That's designed for people who have some experience already.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: I think I need more than that. What else is there?

script.speaker: paula
script.text: The Standard package is twenty hours, at thirty-two pounds an hour, which works out cheaper per hour. It also includes a free motorway lesson, which many schools charge extra for.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: That sounds right for me. And what about the third option?

script.speaker: paula
script.text: The Intensive package is thirty hours, over two or three weeks. It used to cost thirty pounds an hour, but now it's twenty-eight. The price includes the fee for the driving test itself, so you won't have to pay it separately.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: That's tempting, but I can't do so many hours in one go, because of school. I'll go for the Standard package.

script.speaker: paula
script.text: Very good. I'll book your first lesson for next Wednesday at four. Your instructor will be Mr Harris, and he'll pick you up from school.

script.speaker: joel
script.text: Thank you. I'm looking forward to it.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A heritage railway open day
parts.context: A volunteer welcomes visitors to a heritage railway.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear a volunteer welcoming visitors to the open day at a heritage railway. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Millbrook Heritage Railway. My name's Peter Dawson, and I'm one of the volunteers who runs the station. Please look at the map in your programme. We're at the entrance, at the bottom, and the platform is straight ahead.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: As you come in, the ticket office is immediately on your left, next to the path. That's where you can buy your tickets for the steam train. A little further to the left, at the end of the buildings, is the museum, which has a collection of old tickets, uniforms and lamps.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: On the right of the path, the building with the green door is the café, which used to be the waiting room. Beyond it, at the far right on this side of the line, is the model railway. It's one of the biggest in the region, and it's run by a group of retired engineers.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: To reach the other side, use the footbridge at the end of the platform. Directly opposite the entrance, on the north side, is the locomotive shed, where we keep and repair our engines. To the left of it is the signal box, and children are always fascinated by the levers. And on the far right is the picnic area.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: A few facts. The railway is a charity, and our main income comes from ticket sales. Donations help, and the shop contributes a little, but it's the tickets that keep the engines running.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: The train journey takes forty minutes in each direction, and the trains leave every hour. If you'd like to be at the front, where the best views are, please be on the platform ten minutes early.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Today, children can sit in the driver's cab of one of our engines, accompanied by a volunteer. They can't blow the whistle, I'm afraid, because it's very loud, and the neighbours are not so keen.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: One engine is particularly special: Lady Anne. She was built in nineteen twenty-eight, and she appeared in a famous film in the nineteen sixties, which is why she's so popular with visitors.

script.speaker: dawson
script.text: Finally, a safety rule: please stay behind the yellow line on the platform when a train is coming in. You can take photographs, and dogs are welcome on a lead. Now, if you'd like to buy your tickets, the office is just here on the left.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A study on bilingual children
parts.context: Two students plan a research study on children who speak two languages.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two students, Mira and Jonas, planning a research study on bilingual children. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Jonas, how's the literature review for our study on bilingual children going?

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: I've read about thirty papers. The most surprising thing is that bilingual children don't start speaking later than monolingual children, which many parents believe.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: I found something about code-switching, where children switch between languages in one sentence. The old view was that it shows confusion.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: Now the view is that it shows skill, because the child has to know both grammars.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: For our sample, we planned to look at children aged four to six, in two nurseries.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: Only one nursery agreed, though. The other said it would disturb their routine.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Then the sample will be about twenty children from one nursery. We need consent forms from the parents of each child.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: I'll send those out on Monday, with the letter in English and in Polish, because many of the families speak Polish at home.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Good. How long will each child's session be? Dr Evans said no more than fifteen minutes, because young children get tired.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: Fifteen minutes is tight for all the tasks we planned. Let's reduce the number of tasks, rather than rushing them.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Agreed. Quality matters more than quantity.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Let's decide how to describe each method in the methodology chapter. Observation first.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: Watching the children play naturally gives us the richest data. It's by far the most informative method, because they don't know they're being studied.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Then the parent questionnaire.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: Parents tend to exaggerate their child's ability, so I'd say it's unreliable, and we must treat the answers with care.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: The language test?

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: You need training to give it correctly. I haven't had any, so we'll need Dr Evans to show us.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: And interviews with the teachers?

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: They're time-consuming. Each one would take half an hour at least, so we should limit them to three.

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Finally, the drawing task, where the children draw their family and talk about it.

script.speaker: jonas
script.text: That's ideal for young children, because it feels like play, and they relax. Shall I draft the chapter tonight?

script.speaker: mira
script.text: Please. I'll check it tomorrow.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: tidal energy
parts.context: A lecture on how energy can be obtained from the tides.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about tidal energy. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Many renewable energy sources depend on the weather, which is hard to predict. Today I want to talk about one that does not: energy from the tides.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Tides are caused mainly by the gravity of the moon, which pulls the water in the oceans towards it. The sun has a smaller effect. When the sun and the moon are in line, at new moon and full moon, the pull is strongest, and we get very high and very low tides, which are called spring tides.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: There are two main ways of using this energy. The first is the tidal barrage, which is a kind of dam built across an estuary. Water flows in through turbines as the tide rises, and out again as it falls. The first large power station of this kind was built in France, in nineteen sixty-six, and it is still working.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The second method is newer. Tidal stream turbines look like underwater wind turbines. They are placed on the sea floor, where the tidal currents are strong, and the moving water turns the blades. Several can be grouped together in what are called tidal farms.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The great advantage of tidal power is that it is completely predictable. Unlike wind or sunshine, we can calculate the tides decades in advance, so planners know exactly how much electricity to expect, and when.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: But there are problems. First, you need a big difference between high and low tide, a tidal range of at least five metres, and only a few places in the world have that. Second, building a barrage is very expensive. And third, it can change the habitat of the estuary. Fish can be injured by the turbines, and the movement of mud and sand is altered, which affects wildlife.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: For these reasons, tidal stream turbines are now seen as the more promising approach, because they have less effect on the environment. Next week we'll look at wave power.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
